title: Don Norman's Interaction Design Principles
description: Fundamental principles of interaction design from Don Norman's seminal work 'The Design of Everyday Things' and related writings. These principles explain the psychological foundations of how people interact with designed objects and systems, providing a framework for creating intuitive, learnable, and error-tolerant interfaces.
author: Don Norman
primary_source: The Design of Everyday Things (1988, revised 2013)
sources: Norman, D. A. (2013). The Design of Everyday Things: Revised and Expanded Edition. Basic Books.
context: These principles derive from cognitive psychology and human factors research. They explain how people form mental models, perceive affordances, and interact with designed systems. Understanding these principles is fundamental to creating usable interfaces.

principles.name: Affordances
principles.short_description: An affordance is the relationship between the properties of an object and the capabilities of the agent that determine how the object could possibly be used.
principles.detailed_description: Affordances are the possible actions between an object and an agent (typically a person). A chair affords sitting because of its height and flat surface relative to human anatomy. In interface design, affordances are the fundamental properties that determine what actions are possible. However, what matters most in design is perceived affordances - whether users perceive that an action is possible, regardless of whether it actually is.
key_principles: Affordances are relationships between objects and agents
Different agents perceive different affordances
Perceived affordances matter more than actual affordances in design
Good design makes affordances perceivable
Affordances exist independent of user discovery

questions: What actions do interface elements afford?
Are the affordances appropriate for user capabilities?
Can users perceive the affordances?
Do elements afford the actions users expect?
Are false affordances (elements that appear actionable but aren't) avoided?
what_to_look_for: Buttons that look pressable
Links that look clickable
Draggable elements that appear moveable
Input fields that invite text entry
Scrollable areas that suggest more content
Interactive elements distinct from static content

common_violations.example: Static text styled to look like a clickable link
common_violations.impact: Users attempt impossible actions, leading to frustration and confusion

common_violations.example: Clickable elements that don't look interactive
common_violations.impact: Users fail to discover available actions and functionality

common_violations.example: Disabled button that appears enabled, or vice versa
common_violations.impact: User expectations violated, confusion about system state

common_violations.example: Some clickable text is underlined, other clickable text is not
common_violations.impact: Users cannot reliably predict what is actionable

best_practices: Make interactive elements look interactive
Use established conventions for affordances (underlined links, raised buttons)
Ensure non-interactive elements don't appear interactive
Provide visual feedback when hovering over interactive elements
Match visual appearance to functional capabilities
Test whether users recognize affordances without instruction
Use appropriate cursor changes to reinforce affordances
related_concepts: Perceived affordances - what users think is possible
Signifiers - communicate where actions should occur (separate but related)
Anti-affordances - designed to prevent actions

principles.name: Signifiers
principles.short_description: Signifiers communicate where the action should take place. They are signals that indicate what affordances are available and how to access them.
principles.detailed_description: While affordances define what actions are possible, signifiers communicate where and how to perform those actions. A door handle is a signifier that indicates where to grasp and how to operate the door. In digital interfaces, signifiers include labels, icons, highlights, and visual cues that guide users to discover and activate affordances. Good signifiers make the system understandable and usable.
key_principles: Signifiers communicate where actions occur
They indicate how to use affordances
Effective signifiers are perceivable and understandable
Signifiers can be intentional (designed) or unintentional
Good design uses clear, consistent signifiers

questions: Are there clear signifiers for all interactive elements?
Do signifiers clearly indicate what action will occur?
Can users easily discover functionality through signifiers?
Are signifiers consistent across the interface?
Do signifiers match user expectations from prior experience?
what_to_look_for: Clear labels on buttons and controls
Icons that represent their functions
Visual highlights on interactive elements
Hover states showing interactivity
Focus indicators for keyboard navigation
Cursor changes indicating interaction types
Visual cues like arrows, chevrons, or underlines

common_violations.example: Interactive elements with no labels, icons, or visual indication of function
common_violations.impact: Users cannot discover or understand available actions

common_violations.example: Generic icons that could mean multiple things, unclear button labels
common_violations.impact: Users uncertain about what will happen when they act

common_violations.example: Similar actions signified differently in different contexts
common_violations.impact: Users cannot transfer knowledge across interface

common_violations.example: Signifiers that suggest wrong action or outcome
common_violations.impact: Users develop incorrect mental models and make errors

best_practices: Provide clear labels for all interactive elements
Use recognizable icons paired with text when meaning might be ambiguous
Implement consistent signifiers throughout the interface
Use visual hierarchy to indicate primary vs. secondary actions
Provide hover and focus states to confirm interactivity
Follow platform conventions for standard signifiers
Test signifiers with users to ensure they're understood correctly
Use multiple signifiers when appropriate (icon + label + color)
related_concepts: Affordances - what actions are possible
Mappings - relationship between signifiers and their effects
Feedback - confirms that signified action occurred

principles.name: Feedback
principles.short_description: Feedback communicates the results of actions. It is information that confirms the system has received input and shows what effect that input had.
principles.detailed_description: Feedback is essential for users to understand that their actions have been received and what effect they had. It closes the interaction loop by providing information about results. Feedback must be immediate, clear, and informative. Without adequate feedback, users are uncertain whether their actions succeeded, what state the system is in, and what to do next. Good feedback matches the importance and impact of the action.
key_principles: Provide immediate confirmation that actions are received
Communicate results of actions clearly
Match feedback to the importance of the action
Make feedback perceivable but not intrusive
Continuous feedback for ongoing operations

questions: Do all user actions receive timely feedback?
Is feedback clear and informative about what happened?
Is the timing of feedback appropriate (immediate vs. progressive)?
Does feedback match the significance of the action?
Can users understand system state from feedback?
what_to_look_for: Visual confirmation of button clicks and interactions
Progress indicators for ongoing operations
Success and error messages after actions complete
State changes that reflect user actions
Loading indicators for delayed responses
Sound or haptic feedback for important actions (where appropriate)
Visual changes showing system response

common_violations.example: Button click produces no visible response, leaving users uncertain
common_violations.impact: Users don't know if action was received, may click multiple times

common_violations.example: Feedback arrives so late users have moved on or taken other actions
common_violations.impact: Users lose connection between action and result, confusion about cause

common_violations.example: Vague messages like 'Done' without explaining what was accomplished
common_violations.impact: Users uncertain about what actually happened

common_violations.example: Excessive animations, sounds, or messages for minor actions
common_violations.impact: Feedback becomes noise, users learn to ignore it

best_practices: Provide immediate visual feedback for all user actions (within 0.1 seconds)
Show progress indicators for operations taking more than 1 second
Display clear success/error messages after significant actions
Use appropriate feedback modalities (visual, audio, haptic) for context
Make feedback proportional to action importance
Ensure feedback is perceivable but not disruptive to workflow
Provide continuous feedback for ongoing operations
Include enough information so users understand what happened
related_concepts: Visibility of system status (Nielsen's Heuristics)
Immediate vs. eventual feedback
Feed-forward - showing expected results before action is taken

principles.name: Conceptual Models (Mental Models)
principles.short_description: A conceptual model is an explanation of how something works. Users form mental models of systems based on their experience and understanding.
principles.detailed_description: Users create mental models - internal representations of how things work. Good design provides a clear conceptual model through the system image (all information available from the product itself). When the designer's conceptual model matches the user's mental model, the system is intuitive. When they diverge, users struggle. The system image - created through design, documentation, and interaction - is the only communication channel between designer and user.
key_principles: Users form mental models from system image
Designer's model must be communicated through system image
Good design makes conceptual model clear and consistent
Mental models influence predictions and expectations
Inconsistent models lead to confusion and errors

questions: Does the interface clearly communicate how the system works?
Is the conceptual model consistent throughout?
Can users predict system behavior from their mental model?
Does the system image support developing accurate mental models?
Are there conflicting signals about how the system works?
what_to_look_for: Consistent metaphors and terminology
Clear information architecture that reveals structure
Predictable behavior based on established patterns
Documentation and help that explains the conceptual model
Visual structure that reveals functional organization
Consistent cause-and-effect relationships

common_violations.example: System sometimes works like a file system, sometimes like a database, confusing users
common_violations.impact: Users cannot predict behavior, must memorize rather than understand

common_violations.example: Complex system with no clear explanation of how it works
common_violations.impact: Users never develop accurate mental model, rely on trial and error

common_violations.example: Different parts of system suggest different underlying models
common_violations.impact: Users confused about how system actually works

common_violations.example: System image suggests one model but actual behavior follows different rules
common_violations.impact: User expectations violated, errors and frustration

best_practices: Use consistent metaphors throughout the interface (folders, documents, trash, etc.)
Make system structure visible and understandable
Provide clear explanations of how the system works
Ensure behavior matches the suggested conceptual model
Use familiar models when possible (leverage existing user knowledge)
Test whether users develop accurate mental models through use
Document the conceptual model explicitly when complex
Maintain consistency between model and all system behaviors
related_concepts: System image - all perceivable aspects of the system
Designer's model - how designer intends system to work
User's mental model - how user thinks system works
Gulf of evaluation - difficulty understanding system state
Gulf of execution - difficulty determining how to act

principles.name: Constraints
principles.short_description: Constraints limit the possible actions that can be taken. They guide users toward correct actions and prevent errors.
principles.detailed_description: Constraints reduce the number of possible actions at any moment, making interfaces easier to use and errors less likely. There are four types: physical constraints (literal limitations), cultural constraints (conventions), semantic constraints (meaning-based), and logical constraints (reasonable relationships). Good design uses constraints to guide users naturally toward correct actions without explicit instruction.
key_principles: Constraints limit possibilities to reduce errors
Different types serve different purposes
Good constraints feel natural, not restrictive
Constraints guide without explicit instruction
Use constraints to prevent errors rather than recover from them

physical.description: Physical limitations that prevent wrong actions
digital_examples: Input fields that only accept certain characters
Drag targets that only accept compatible items
Disabled buttons when actions aren't available
Red for stop/error, green for go/success
Icons with conventional meanings (trash for delete)
Email field requires valid email format
Date picker prevents selecting dates in the past
Password field requires certain character types
Next button disabled until current step complete
Undo only available after an action is taken
Save only enabled when changes have been made

questions: Are constraints used to prevent common errors?
Do constraints feel natural and helpful rather than arbitrary?
Are impossible actions prevented rather than just warned against?
Do constraints leverage physical, cultural, semantic, or logical principles?
Are constraints clear enough that users understand why they exist?
what_to_look_for: Disabled controls when actions aren't appropriate
Input validation preventing invalid data
Drag-and-drop that only allows valid combinations
Form fields that guide correct input format
Stepped processes that prevent skipping necessary steps
Visual or interactive limitations that match business rules

common_violations.example: Allowing users to enter invalid data then showing error after submission
common_violations.impact: Errors that could have been prevented occur frequently

common_violations.example: Limiting actions without clear reason or benefit
common_violations.impact: Users frustrated by unnecessary limitations

common_violations.example: Some email fields validate format, others don't until submission
common_violations.impact: Users uncertain about what's actually required or allowed

common_violations.example: Preventing actions without explaining why they're not available
common_violations.impact: Users confused about why they can't do what they expect

best_practices: Use constraints to prevent errors rather than reporting them after the fact
Disable unavailable options rather than showing errors when selected
Provide input masking for formatted data (phone numbers, credit cards)
Use appropriate input types that constrain naturally (date pickers, dropdowns)
Make constraints perceivable - show why options are unavailable
Leverage cultural conventions (color meanings, icon conventions)
Apply semantic constraints based on meaning (email format, positive numbers)
Use logical constraints based on reasonable relationships (next after current)
related_concepts: Error prevention (Nielsen's Heuristics)
Forcing functions - constraints that prevent proceeding without completing required actions
Poka-yoke - mistake-proofing from manufacturing

principles.name: Mapping
principles.short_description: Mapping is the relationship between controls and their effects. Good mappings are natural and intuitive, making the relationship between actions and results clear.
principles.detailed_description: Mapping describes the relationship between the layout and arrangement of controls and their effects in the world. Natural mappings leverage spatial relationships, cultural standards, and analogies to create intuitive interfaces. When mapping is good, users immediately understand what control affects what outcome. Poor mapping requires labels, instructions, or memory to use successfully.
key_principles: Natural mappings leverage spatial relationships
Good mappings make effects of controls immediately obvious
Cultural standards provide conventional mappings
Physical analogies create intuitive mappings
Poor mapping requires labels and memory

questions: Is the relationship between controls and effects clear?
Do spatial arrangements match expected relationships?
Can users predict effects from control layout?
Are cultural conventions followed for mappings?
Do controls require labels to understand their effects?
what_to_look_for: Spatial correspondence between controls and affected elements
Controls arranged to match layout of what they control
Use of natural analogies (sliders for continuous values)
Cultural conventions (up/right for increase, down/left for decrease)
Proximity of controls to affected elements
Visual connections showing relationships

common_violations.example: Volume controls where left button increases and right decreases
common_violations.impact: Users must memorize mapping, frequent errors

common_violations.example: Controls arranged differently than elements they affect
common_violations.impact: Users cannot predict which control affects which element

common_violations.example: Green for stop, red for go
common_violations.impact: Strong learned associations violated, high error rate

common_violations.example: Control panel far from elements it affects with no visual connection
common_violations.impact: Relationship between control and effect unclear

best_practices: Arrange controls to match spatial layout of affected elements
Use natural mappings when possible (sliders for ranges, toggles for binary states)
Follow cultural conventions for directional relationships
Place controls near the elements they affect
Use visual connections (lines, grouping) to show relationships
Leverage physical analogies from real world
Test mappings with users to ensure they're intuitive
Avoid requiring labels to understand control-effect relationships
related_concepts: Natural mapping - relationships that require no learning
Spatial correspondence - layout matching physical arrangement
Logical mapping - meaningful non-spatial relationships

principles.name: Consistency
principles.short_description: Consistency means that similar operations and elements should behave and appear similarly. It allows users to transfer knowledge across contexts.
principles.detailed_description: Consistency enables transfer of learning. When similar things work similarly, users can apply knowledge from one context to another. There are multiple levels: internal consistency (within the product), external consistency (with platform conventions), and consistency with user expectations from domain knowledge. Consistency reduces cognitive load and learning time while increasing predictability and efficiency.
key_principles: Similar things should look and behave similarly
Consistency enables knowledge transfer
Multiple levels: internal, external, and domain consistency
Consistency reduces learning time and cognitive load
Break consistency only when there's clear benefit

internal.description: Consistency within the product or system
examples: Same button styles for similar actions throughout

external.description: Consistency with platform conventions and standards
examples: Following iOS or Android design guidelines

domain.description: Consistency with industry or domain standards
examples: Using standard medical terminology in health apps
Following financial industry conventions in banking apps
Matching genre conventions in games or creative tools

questions: Do similar elements behave similarly throughout?
Is terminology used consistently?
Does the interface follow platform conventions?
Are interaction patterns consistent across features?
Do similar situations present similar interfaces?
what_to_look_for: Uniform button styles and behaviors
Consistent terminology throughout
Standard icon meanings maintained
Similar layouts for similar content types
Consistent interaction patterns
Following platform guidelines
Matching user expectations from similar products

common_violations.example: Calling same action 'delete', 'remove', and 'discard' in different places
common_violations.impact: Users uncertain whether these are different actions or same one

common_violations.example: Primary buttons styled differently across screens
common_violations.impact: Users can't reliably identify primary actions

common_violations.example: Some buttons execute immediately, others show confirmation, without clear pattern
common_violations.impact: Users uncertain about what will happen, hesitant to act

common_violations.example: Using non-standard gestures or shortcuts that conflict with platform norms
common_violations.impact: User muscle memory from platform violated, frequent errors

best_practices: Create and maintain design systems for consistent components
Use consistent terminology documented in style guide
Follow platform guidelines for your target systems
Maintain consistent interaction patterns across features
Use standard icons with conventional meanings
Keep visual styling uniform for similar elements
Document and communicate consistency standards to team
Break consistency only when there's clear user benefit
Test cross-feature consistency systematically
related_concepts: Consistency and Standards (Nielsen's Heuristics)
Design systems and pattern libraries
Platform guidelines (Material Design, Human Interface Guidelines)

seven_stages_of_action.description: Norman's model of how people interact with systems, forming two gulfs that design must bridge.

stages.description: Form the goal - what do I want to accomplish?
Form the intention - what actions will achieve the goal?
Specify the action sequence - what specific actions?
Execute the action - physically perform the action
Interpret the perception - what does it mean?
Compare outcome with goal - did I achieve what I wanted?

gulf_of_execution.description: The gap between user intentions and allowable actions. How hard is it to figure out how to do what you want?

gulf_of_evaluation.description: The gap between system state and user understanding. How hard is it to figure out what happened?

design_implications.discoverability: Users can discover what actions are possible (good signifiers, visible affordances)
design_implications.understanding: Users can understand the system (clear conceptual model, good feedback)
design_implications.learnability: Users can learn how to use the system (consistency, good mappings)
design_implications.error_tolerance: System prevents errors and supports recovery (constraints, feedback, undo)

how_to_apply: 1. Analyze each interaction through the seven stages of action
2. Evaluate interface against each principle systematically
3. Identify where gulfs of execution and evaluation are largest
4. Apply principles to bridge gulfs and improve interactions
5. Test with users to verify improvements

evaluation_approach.heuristic_evaluation: Walk through interface asking evaluation questions for each principle
evaluation_approach.cognitive_walkthrough: Trace user goals through seven stages of action
evaluation_approach.usability_testing: Observe where users struggle and map to principle violations

design_process_integration: Early design: Use principles to evaluate concepts and sketches
Detailed design: Apply principles to specific interaction patterns
Implementation: Ensure principles maintained in final product
Testing: Use principles to structure usability evaluation
Iteration: Apply principles to identify and fix problems

relationship_to_other_frameworks.nielsen_heuristics: Tactical evaluation guidelines complementing Norman's theoretical foundations
relationship_to_other_frameworks.rams_principles: Broader design philosophy that these interaction principles help achieve
relationship_to_other_frameworks.gestalt_principles: Perceptual principles underlying visual design aspects
relationship_to_other_frameworks.fitts_law: Specific interaction principle about target size and distance
relationship_to_other_frameworks.hicks_law: Principle about choice and decision time complementing constraint principle
